content.text: Some see the U.S. airstrikes as liberation from a vicious dictator. Others call it another example of American imperialism. SEATTLE — There is no single consensus among Iranian Americans in western Washington following the death of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in joint U.S.-Israeli airstrikes, with some celebrating what they call liberation while others condemning the strikes as reckless imperialism. Just hours after news broke Saturday that Khamenei had been killed, hundreds of Iranian Americans took to the streets of Bellevue in celebration. At a car rally on the interstate organized by Voice of Iran, demonstrators waved pre-revolutionary Iranian flags and chanted in support of President Donald Trump’s military action. The rally moved to a downtown Bellevue park, where celebrations continued. “Someone just showed me the phone and said, he’s dead. He’s dead,” recalled Arash, who organized the rally. “There is some video. You can find it even online — it’s me jumping up and down with megaphone and telling people he’s gone. He’s gone.” Arash spoke to KING 5 at Rose Market, an Iranian and Persian grocery store in Bellevue owned by his friend Hadi Sadghnezhd. Both men fled Iran more than a decade ago to escape religious and political persecution, and for them, Khamenei’s death represents the end of decades of brutality. “We had this regime killing people right and left for years,” Arash said Tuesday at the grocery store, where the pre-revolutionary Iranian flag hangs prominently. “It’s really meaningful for us to get rid of the dictatorship in Iran. The future is going to be bright.” The jubilation, however, has not been universal. At Pike Place Market on Saturday, protesters gathered to denounce the U.S. and Israeli airstrikes. Meanwhile, celebrations in Bellevue turned tense when police began investigating reports that someone brandished a gun at demonstrators. Saghar Amini, a demonstrator who filmed the interaction, said one man grabbed his two young children and ran for safety. “[The man] told [a demonstrator] that he intended to shoot. He told him, ‘Don’t come any closer or I’ll shoot,’” Amini said. At the University of Washington, Aria Fani, director of the Middle East Center at the Jackson School of International Studies, expressed alarm at the rapidly escalating conflict. “I’m going crazy. I cannot control my — I’m just running around impulsively,” Fani said in an interview. “I’m worried. I’m worried so much for people there.” Fani, who was born and raised in Iran and has family there, sharply criticized the military intervention, questioning why anyone would support the bombardment of civilian infrastructure. “Why would anybody favor bombardment of hospitals? Schools?” he asked. “Who would be for this? It’s total perversion.” The divide centers on fundamentally different interpretations of U.S. involvement. At Rose Market, where Iranian customers have been coming in with renewed hope since Khamenei’s death, Arash framed the military action as necessary intervention. “This is not war. This is a rescue mission,” he said. He expressed confidence in Trump’s leadership and gratitude for U.S. involvement. “Iranian community, even Iranian people inside Iran, they are thankful of President Trump,” he said. But Fani sees a dangerous pattern repeating itself. “I think the U.S. loves when brown people dance on the street, having been liberated by its military power,” he said. “We saw this on the streets of Baghdad when Saddam Hussein fell. And then what? What we didn’t know was a million people were going to lose their lives.” He compared the current situation to past U.S. interventions in the Middle East, questioning whether any have ended well. “When has this ended well? Point to an example. I’ll get on board,” Fani said. For some Iranian Americans, the uncertain succession offers hope for democratic change. Arash said he believes opposition leader Reza Pahlavi will return to Iran to help establish free elections. “Both of us and both countries are going to be friends again, just like before 1979,” he said. “Iran is going to be a very reliable ally for us.” Others worry the power vacuum will lead to more violence and instability. Fani said he hasn’t been able to reach family members in Iran. “Nobody’s OK. Nobody’s OK when bombs are falling,” he said. He added: “It’s really not courageous to celebrate from the safety of Bellevue. The real courage would be to celebrate on the streets of Tehran when the bombs are falling.”
